Paper:
title: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent's task capability while reinforcing behavior that violates contextual execution requirements. We study this reward-driven misalignment, including reward hacking, through verifiable reward--context conflicts, where compliant task completion remains feasible while some executable shortcuts earn more reward than every compliant strategy. Encoding these conflicts in task dynamics lets us generate diverse interactive environments at scale and derive compliance feedback from execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual work declines. Controlled changes in the training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9\% certified profitable violations on an API task under a 25\% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32 unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from 53.1\% to 89.1\% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work. These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution requirements.

Paper:
title: TUTTI: Parallel CKKS Bootstrapping in under 3 ms on CPU
summary: This paper introduces TUTTI, a new CKKS bootstrapping procedure that outperforms previous low-latency solutions in multi-threaded latency for any number of messages and, most notably, has a lower latency than TFHE when bootstrapping a single one. Our bootstrapping builds upon SPRU (CK, TCHES 2027), improving it with new methods for exploiting parallelism and increasing the number of messages, as well as with a refined security analysis, of independent interest, of the block-binary secret keys of LMSS (AsiaCCS 2023). TUTTI bootstraps 4096 real-number messages in 46 to 83.4 ms on 192 threads to restore 1 to 9 multiplicative levels, outperforming SHIP (CHKS, Eurocrypt 2025) by a factor of up to 3 on the same machine. Unlike SHIP, TUTTI gains immediately from bootstrapping fewer messages, with a 256-message bootstrapping taking just 15 to 34 ms on 32 threads. For a single message, TUTTI takes 4.6 ms on 32 threads, whereas TFHE-rs needs 7.3 ms for a 4-bit bootstrapping on the same machine and thread count. We show that this advantage persists across different architectures: on an Apple M5 Pro laptop (ARM), TUTTI takes 2.4 ms on 14 threads, against 4.5 ms for TFHE-rs. Differences between CKKS and lightweight schemes such as TFHE remain on several fronts, from functionality to key sizes and security assumptions, but our work shows that multi-threaded latency is no longer one of them, closing a long-standing gap in the practical FHE literature.

Paper:
title: Contention Resolution with a Fast-but-Fickle Channel
summary: The contention-resolution problem studies how $n$ devices share a communication channel without centralized coordination. Classical models typically assume a single continuously available channel and focus on minimizing total completion time. However, modern wireless systems increasingly rely on shared spectrum, where access may be abruptly revoked by incumbent users.
  Motivated by this setting, we study contention resolution with two channels: a reliable slow channel and a faster channel that can be intermittently disabled by unpredictable eviction periods. Moving a batch of packets from the slow channel to the fast channel incurs a unit cost, while evictions from the fast channel impose a larger per-packet penalty. Our goal is to achieve asymptotically optimal latency while minimizing switching overhead relative to an optimal offline algorithm that knows the eviction schedule.
  We present Randomized Adaptive Channel Exploitation (RACE), a randomized algorithm that exploits the fast channel when available while maintaining progress on the slow channel during disruptions. When the fast channel has rate $ρ\in \bigl[Ω(\log n), O(\sqrt n)\bigr]$ and a sufficiently large constant-factor resource augmentation, RACE achieves an $O(1)$ competitive ratio for expected latency. RACE's expected switching-cost competitive ratio relative to any optimal-latency offline algorithm OPT is $O(ρ+\sqrt{n/m})$, where $m \geq 1$ is the number of fast-channel availability intervals used by OPT.
  We also prove a worst-case $Ω(\sqrt n)$ switching-cost competitive ratio for latency-competitive randomized algorithms, and a separate $Ω(ρ)$ switching-cost competitive-ratio lower bound. These lower bounds hold even with fixed constant-factor augmentation on both channels.

Paper:
title: Suppression Is Not Erasure: Mechanistic Analysis and Reactivation Boundaries of Subspace Projection for LoRA Backdoor Defense
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is the standard paradigm for customizing large language models, yet third-party LoRA adapters pose a supply-chain risk: modifying less than 1% of model parameters suffices to implant stealthy backdoors. Recent defenses project adapter weights onto estimated backdoor subspaces, reporting near-zero static Attack Success Rates (ASR). We audit subspace-projection defenses across four model scales (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B) and three architectures (Qwen2.5, InternLM2.5, Spark). Constructively, module-wise rank-1 trigger-difference projection (k=1, alpha=1) reduces ASR from 60.4% to 0.0% on standard benchmarks and from 70.3% to 0.0% on a 1,000-sample uncontaminated suite (p = 3.055e-299, instruction-level p = 9.49e-16) in under 5 seconds end-to-end, and we prove via a spectral-gap bound why trigger-free calibration with benign polite suffixes aligns with u1(B) (median cosine 0.9048) and achieves 0.0% ASR without prior trigger knowledge. Our main contribution is a negative finding: static ASR reduction does not imply parameter erasure. Under 5-sample few-shot reactivation, every evaluated weight-editing defense rebounds (91.7%-100.0% ASR in 1 epoch for standard projections, Fine-Pruning, ANP, SVD truncation and Li & Kim's dual-end projection; 48.7% for our single-round dual variant), all reaching 100.0% by Epoch 2, with first-epoch loss up to 5.7x lower than training from scratch. Using an exact spectrum-preserving Haar orthogonal rotation control (Frobenius norm 10.0928 preserved to 1.70e-6) and N=1..6 cumulative Gram-Schmidt basis ablation, we decompose reactivation into residual trigger-difference coupling energy at Epoch 1 (Spearman rho = 0.986), base-model learnability at Epoch 2 (100%), and benign semantic direction conflict (41.7%).

Paper:
title: DeepChronos: Temporal Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Multi-Step Attack Detection
summary: Modern cyber threats commonly unfold as multi-step attacks comprising temporally and causally related phases. Current defenses commonly follow a detect first and correlate later paradigm. Intrusion detection systems classify events independently, while downstream systems reconstruct attack progression from the resulting alerts or audit records. In this context, learning-based detectors learn attack-step dependencies implicitly as statistical regularities in the data and cannot guarantee that their predictions follow the real attack progression. Conversely, correlation systems represent attack relationships explicitly, but apply this knowledge only after the underlying attack observations have been detected. We present DEEPCHRONOS, a neuro-symbolic network intrusion detection system that shifts the paradigm from detect first and correlate later to detection through logical progression. DEEPCHRONOS combines learned flow-level evidence with explicit attack-phase rules, temporal prerequisites, and previously inferred phases, allowing the evolving attack history to inform and constrain each detection decision. Evaluations on DARPA 2000 and AIT-LDS V2 show that DEEPCHRONOS improves macro F1 over purely neural baselines by up to 11.3%, eliminates causal violations under strict temporal constraints, and maintains millisecond-scale inference latency. These results demonstrate that integrating explicit attack progression knowledge into detection produces more accurate and temporally coherent multi-step attack predictions.

Paper:
title: The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort
summary: Package hallucinations, LLM-generated references to packages that do not exist, enable slopsquatting: an attacker registers the hallucinated name. We replicate Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security '25) on five 2026 frontier models over 199,840 Python and JavaScript generations. This version reports a preregistered live revalidation that replaces the static package lists of earlier versions with two independent checks against the live PyPI and npm registries. Hallucination rates are 3.6-5.0% of package mentions (2.2-3.4% of generations): the 2026 frontier sits at the level of 2024's commercial models, and the open-weight gap seen in 2024 has disappeared. Python exceeds JavaScript for every model. The set of names hallucinated by all five models shrinks from the 127 reported earlier to 104; 26 earlier entries were correct import statements whose module name differs from the package name. Using the accidental six-month public exposure of our own list as a natural experiment, we find no detectable effect of publication: about 1% of hallucinated names were registered within six months, at the same rate for published and unpublished names, and the 95% interval excludes increases above 2.5 percentage points. Still, at least 23 package names that the models suggest had previously hosted malware later removed by the registries, and one hallucinated name was registered with malware after our runs.

Paper:
title: Checking DER Commands Against Grid Context Catches Credentialed Attacks Static Checks Miss
summary: Authorization of distributed energy resource (DER) commands judges a command by who sent it and whether its value has been seen before. An attacker holding a legitimate credential who writes ordinary values passes both tests. We add a check that judges each DER write against the grid's operating context: the bus voltages around the target, the hour, the day- ahead price, system load, and irradiance, compared with what operators wrote under similar conditions in the feeder's own benign history. We evaluate it live on the IEEE 123-bus and 8500-node feeders, driven by a measured 2024 year of price, load, and irradiance, against nine attack scenarios. A lookup trained on the same history catches none of the writes of the four scenarios that send values already familiar on the targeted device; the context check refuses 91.7% of insider-abuse writes and 64.4% of DER-aggregation writes while denying 1.28% of benign writes. In an offline test that replays recorded moments with curtailment setpoints drawn from the benign range, issued at a positive price, it refuses 47.3% and 50.5% on the two feeders, against 18.5% and 16.0% for the same check without context; live, the few setpoints tested were mostly shallow and were mostly allowed. The context check complements the lookup.

Paper:
title: SlotGuard: Stop Oversharing Private Local Context in LLM Agent Transcripts
summary: LLM agents can expose private local context (e.g., paths, emails) and credentials (e.g., API keys) as agent observations (e.g., tool outputs, shell logs, and file reads) are appended to provider-bound transcripts. Existing placeholder redaction is brittle: it can miss embedded or cross-turn references, over-redact benign lookalikes, and destroy the structure useful for reasoning. We present SlotGuard, a local transcript boundary that can hide sensitive data while retaining agents' performance. SlotGuard rewrites structural bindings as typed, suffix-aware slots, replaces secrets with format-preserving synthetic values, links cross-turn references with a lightweight session graph, and restores raw values only inside the trusted runtime. On controlled repository-oriented agent transcripts, SlotGuard removes all 20,814 annotated structurally sensitive characters across 9,229 paths and reduces credential leakage to 0.0% across 852 planted values. It remains close to raw-transcript task success across four upstream models, while generic redaction drops to 2.5%. Deterministic transcript rewriting takes a median of 14.424 microseconds per agent turn, excluding the optional semantic detector. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/illinoisdata/SlotGuard.
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17147v2

Paper:
title: Maurer-Inspired Two-Way Physical-Layer Authentication Against Multi-Antenna Impersonation Attacks
summary: In this work, we investigate Maurer-inspired two-way physical-layer authentication. Alice seeks authentication by Bob in the presence of a multi-antenna impersonator, Trudy. Trudy may replace the challenge to Alice, the response to Bob, or both. To create an information advantage, Bob adds artificial noise (AN) to his challenge, and Alice adds spatial AN while forwarding the received mixture. Bob predicts the response from trusted preparation, whereas Trudy observes only a noisy version of the challenge, and Alice's AN interferes with Trudy's preparation reception. Impersonation thus requires matching Bob's fresh randomness beyond the channel consistency checked by public-pilot one-way authentication. For quasi-static Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output channels with time-division duplex (TDD) reciprocity, we derive missed-detection bounds for attacks that replace the authentication challenge, the response, or both. These bounds assume attack-free initial training and preparation and account for estimation error and AN leakage. With equal antenna numbers at all nodes, we show scenarios where the proposed scheme has lower worst-case missed detection than specified one-way tests with/without AN.
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12648v1

Paper:
title: BioBind: Binding Biometric Deduplication to Zero-Knowledge Authentication
summary: Biometric identity systems for decentralized applications need credentials that resist repeated enrollment and support private, publicly verifiable authentication. Capture and large-scale private deduplication run off chain while smart contracts authorize issuance and use; these stages span distinct trust domains, and a correct verdict covers only the checked inputs and gallery snapshot. Without binding and state checks, concurrent enrollments can issue duplicate credentials from correct verdicts, while substituted inputs can authorize unrelated credentials. We present BioBind, a protocol whose four backend interface conditions bind the deduplication query, gallery insertion and issued commitment to one captured vector, authenticate gallery transitions, and require a sound uniqueness verdict valid at finalization. Its encrypted instance uses bound requests, stale-session rejection and committee-confirmed migration. Capture-bound zero-knowledge authentication links credential use to the enrolled template and a fresh device-originated probe bound to the challenge. We give a conditional multi-session composition argument under explicit capture, backend and cryptographic assumptions. A prototype using LFW face features rejects the tested composition attacks; its unlinkable authentication circuit uses 31,445 constraints and about 305,000 gas. An equal-public-field baseline quantifies the cost of verifiable matching: witness-plus-proving medians are 1.989 s versus 1.119 s with device-trusted matching. Separate tests of encrypted enrollment complete three histories of 16,384 registrations without decoding errors at the tested checkpoints. Biometric accuracy bounds person-level uniqueness: on the Bosphorus database, cooperative subjects who change appearance evade deduplication in 1.8% of re-enrollment attempts at the operating threshold. Full backend integration remains open.

Paper:
title: Internet-Scale Measurement of React2Shell Exploitation Using an Active Network Telescope
summary: The increasing adoption of server-side component-based web frameworks has introduced new application-layer attack surfaces that remain insufficiently understood at Internet scale. On 3 December 2025, a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2025-55182) in React Server Components, referred to as React2Shell, was publicly disclosed and subsequently observed being exploited in the wild. Despite its critical severity and a CVSS base score of 10.0, there is limited empirical understanding of how this vulnerability is exploited across the Internet. This paper presents the first Internet-scale measurement study of React2Shell exploitation activity using traffic collected from an Active Network Telescope. We developed a deterministic detection methodology that identifies exploitation attempts targeting endpoints implementing React Server components. It helped analyze exploitation traffic to characterize its temporal evolution, geographic and autonomous system-level distribution, and behavioral properties of the observed scanning activity. In addition, exploit payloads are examined to understand the attacker infrastructure and delivery mechanisms. The analysis reported rapid post-disclosure exploitation activity exhibiting patterns consistent with automated scanning campaigns, geographically distributed scanners, and concentrated backend infrastructure. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first quantitative characterization of React2Shell-triggered scanning activity, including the number of distinct scanners, their geographic and autonomous system distribution, and the scale of backend infrastructure involved in exploitation attempts.

Paper:
title: How Far Does Second-Order Linear Response Predict Quantization Mismatch? Pre-Registered Measurements on Five Language Models
summary: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12Δ^\top FΔ$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $α^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.

Paper:
title: LLM Watermarking as Big Data Provenance: A Deployment-Oriented Systematization
summary: As large language models (LLMs) generate and transform content at scale, reliable attribution becomes an increasingly important requirement for big data provenance. Although numerous watermarking methods have been proposed, existing evaluations predominantly emphasize sample-level detectability and robustness, leaving deployment requirements such as serving efficiency, population-scale false positives, multi-key attribution, and long-term verification less systematically examined. This paper presents a deployment-oriented systematization of LLM watermarking through the five Vs of big data: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, and Value. We classify representative watermarking methods across four dimensions: insertion point, verification authority, operational state, and adversarial threat model. We further map these methods to four deployment workloads: online generation, streaming detection, transformation pipelines, and ecosystem governance. Our synthesis identifies recurring limitations, including dependencies on generation-time access, additional inference overhead, sensitivity to downstream transformations, and incomplete reporting of calibration and lifecycle compatibility. Based on these findings, we propose workload-specific evaluation requirements covering statistical reliability, throughput, utility, robustness, and governance. This framework connects watermark design choices to practical deployment constraints and provides guidance for selecting and evaluating provenance mechanisms in large-scale data ecosystems.

Paper:
title: Reconfiguring System-Level Protection Through Bounded Delegation in RISC-V MCUs
summary: MCU-based embedded and cyber-physical systems increasingly require protection policies to change at runtime as resources, software, and system composition evolve. Yet widely used COTS MCU protection mechanisms are still largely designed around statically established policies. While they can restrict which domains modify protection primitives, they generally do not constrain what policy an authorized domain may create. As a result, domains may expand protection rules beyond their intended scope or interfere with boundaries established by other domains. We identify bounded configuration authority as a missing primitive for secure dynamic policy evolution and introduce an ownership-aware model in which explicit ownership and rule containment bound both configuration authority and recursive delegation. Changes to active protection-rule ranges are validated before commit, preserving protection boundaries without extending the normal access-checking datapath. We implement the model in an open-source RISC-V World Checker integrated into a CVA6-based SoC. Our FPGA evaluation shows no degradation in access latency or operating frequency, with 7.1% LUT and 1.2% FF overhead for eight rules. In an OTA update case study, direct reconfiguration under delegated authority reduces policy-transition latency by 89.5% over hypervisor mediation and 94.6% over trusted firmware mediation, while preserving established authority boundaries. All artifacts will be open-sourced to support the evolution of RISC-V specifications and system-level protection designs.

Paper:
title: Double Blind Evals: Resolving the Dual Confidentiality Dilemma in AI Safety Auditing
summary: AI safety evaluations often involve sensitive prompts and proprietary models. Evaluators want to keep their evaluation prompts secret from model owners to prevent purposeful or incidental data leakage, ensuring longer usefulness of their benchmark. Model owners in turn wish to keep their proprietary model weights and inference code within their own secure infrastructure to protect their IP. We present a way forward for "double-blind evals", which provide cryptographic guarantees that an evaluator's prompts are not shared with the model owner, while simultaneously maintaining the confidentiality of the model weights and inference code. To accomplish this, we use secure enclaves that encrypt data in RAM at the hardware level. In a world-first pilot, we test this approach by evaluating a proprietary Google DeepMind model (Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite) against a selection of the private AILuminate benchmark corpus, using an NVIDIA H100 secure enclave on Google Cloud Platform, and using OpenMined's PySyft to maintain data and model privacy. We believe this effort marks the first use of this technology to provide mutual secrecy for one organization's frontier-class proprietary model weights and another organization's closed benchmark.

Paper:
title: Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
summary: In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur ($\mathsf{dQMA}$) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to $k$ unentangled provers, denoted by $\mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$. In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers.
  Our first result reduces the number of provers from $k$ to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from $k$ to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding $\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$.

Paper:
title: Covert System Identification Under Timing Constraints: A Static Linear Model and Its Detectability Implications
summary: This paper studies covert system identification in cyber-physical systems, where an attacker infers plant dynamics while attempting to remain stealthy. We introduce a lightweight static linear model in which the time to execute a setpoint change is proportional to the commanded speed difference. On a Siemens PROFINET testbed this gain captures the drive's ramp response accurately but not its terminal overshoot. That omitted transient becomes the attacker's main exposure: on real traces, the residual left by the linear masking procedure is detected by two anomaly monitors, Process-Aware Stealthy-Attack Detection (PASAD) and the CUSUM change detector. Across the cascade identification and staircase attack strategies defined in the paper, the stealth boundary relates to the plant's own settling transients, a structural limit for this class of models under the adopted detector-calibration regime. Comparison against dynamic models obtained by N4SID, trained at multiple excitation amplitudes, shows that the evaluated N4SID models do not improve stealth over the structure-informed ramp model. Since per-cycle computation is negligible for both procedures, the binding trade-off is not inference cost but whether the attacker can acquire and refresh a model without injecting detectable perturbations.

title: Text2NGAC: a multi-LLM pipeline for NGAC policy extraction with mutation-based verification
summary: Access-control policies are written in natural language but enforced as formal models, and translating them into NIST Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) graphs remains unsolved: prior systems cover only subsets of the NGAC model, and none verify the graphs they extract. We present Text2NGAC, a pipeline of cooperating large language models that disambiguates each sentence before extraction, escalates uncertain sentences to a multi-model ensemble, and checks the resulting graph with a five-strategy verifier whose own effectiveness is measured by controlled mutation testing. To our knowledge it is the first system to extract all four NGAC relationship types - associations, prohibitions, event-response obligations, and assignments - from real-world policy documents. Three results anchor the evaluation. The verifier detects 99.7% of 918 injected mutants and every structural fail-open fault, and the fault classes it misses are characterized and weighted by security consequence rather than left unexamined. The extracted graphs are enforceable: one corpus's graph loads unmodified into the NIST reference implementation, which reproduces all 55 access decisions the graph entails and fires an extracted obligation end-to-end. Extraction reaches 97.3-99.6% exact-tuple-match accuracy on the 714 scored sentences of four real corpora, far above three reproduced baselines on matched metrics, and paraphrase probes with semantic re-scoring bound the pipeline's sensitivity to rewording. Reported accuracy is wording- and benchmark-specific, adversarial input is outside the verifier's guarantees, and the intended deployment is extraction plus structural verification feeding expert review. A complete two-tier reproducibility artifact accompanies the paper.
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12572v1

Paper:
title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Privacy-Enhanced Computing Through Register Renaming
summary: Privacy-Enhanced Computing (PEC) is a mechanism to hide program secrets from the outside world without paying the cost of fully-homomorphic encryption. Previous work has developed hardware mechanisms to achieve this goal but they require a dedicated processor enclave where all computations are done, requiring duplicate ALU resources and limiting the performance of PEC-utilizing applications due to not being able to access the full compute resources of the processor (e.g., multiple execution units and vector units), or not being able to execute PEC instructions in parallel and out-of-order.
  In this work, we introduce HPS-PEC (Hidden in Plain Sight PEC), a novel method of utilizing existing infrastructure in the CPU to achieve PEC with minor modifications to the architecture. We show that, across 25 VIP-Bench benchmarks and with a 7-cycle QARMA-64 cipher, HPS-PEC runs encrypted code at 3.41x the execution time of unprotected native code (geometric mean), of which 1.03x is the cost of data-oblivious code itself, and is 1.26x faster than a Sequestered Encryption (SE) unit while utilizing under a third of its dedicated area. Our method keeps plaintext out of reach of every instruction, as an enclave does given a correctly functioning renamer and register file, which every program already depends on.

Paper:
title: Leader Election via Unique Sink Orientation
summary: A proof-labeling scheme (PLS) certifies a global property using only local checks. That is, a prover assigns a certificate to every node and each node accepts or rejects by inspecting only the certificates in its neighborhood, so that every graph satisfying some global property admits a certificate assignment accepted by all nodes (existence) and every certificate assignment accepted by all nodes gives a legal configuration (soundness). In this work, we design PLSs for two classical problems, leader certification and spanning tree certification, assuming that all nodes are anonymous, for a specific class of graphs. Certifying a unique leader is impossible in general anonymous graphs for any certificate size due to a well-known result for rings by [Korman, Kutten and Peleg, 2010]. This raises the question of which graph classes admit a PLS for leader certification with anonymous nodes, ideally with size independent of the size of the graph. Our work contributes to a growing list of such classes, which includes chordal graphs, meshed graphs and simply connected subsets of the triangular grid. We consider dismantlable graphs, a class which contains trees, chordal, bridged and Helly graphs, as well as the $k$-th powers of $δ$-hyperbolic graphs for $k \geq 2δ$. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first PLSs tailored to dismantlable graphs, potentially highlighting structural properties useful for certifying additional problems. Finally, we present a generic transformation that converts any labeling scheme with certificates of finite type into a silent self-stabilizing algorithm by adding only one extra state, assuming a Gouda fair scheduler, whereas known generic transformations require $O(\ell + \log n)$ bits for $\ell$-bit certificates. This transformation may be of independent interest.

Paper:
title: A decomposition approach for large virtual network embedding
summary: Virtual Network Embedding (VNE) is the core combinatorial problem of Network Slicing, a 5G technology which enables telecommunication operators to propose diverse service-dedicated virtual networks, embedded onto a common substrate network. VNE asks for a minimum-cost mapping of a virtual network on a substrate network, encompassing simultaneous node placement and edge routing decisions. On a benchmark of large virtual networks with realistic topologies we compiled, the state-of-the art heuristics often provide expensive solutions, or even fail to find a solution when resources are sparse. We introduce a new integer linear formulation together with a decomposition scheme based on an automatic partition of the virtual network. This results in a column generation approach whose pricing problems are also VNE problems. This method allows to compute better lower bounds than state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we devise an efficient Price-and-Branch heuristic for large instances.

Paper:
title: ML Models Are Not Ciphers: Power Analysis for Weight Extraction Is Harder Than You Think
summary: Can power-analysis techniques reveal secret weights of machine-learning models? Multiple recent works demonstrate proof-of-concept attacks that can partially recover such weights. To that end, these works build on techniques from cryptographic engineering, treating the model as a ``cipher'' and its secret weights as keys.
  We question the basic assumption behind such straightforward adaptations of cryptographic attacks and highlight the challenges arising when applying past techniques to fully recover all layers of deep neural networks. Unlike past works, which extract only a few weights, typically from shallow layers, we investigate the recovery of complete networks. Moreover, we target fully trained and functional models, rather than untrained, randomly initialized networks. To focus on fundamental challenges, we assume an unrealistically strong side-channel adversary that can directly observe the output of the leakage model without any added noise. With this adversary, we show that machine-learning models differ significantly from cryptographic implementations, giving rise to unique challenges that have not been observed in the prior art.
  We observe two main differences between machine-learning models and ciphers. First, in contrast to the high-diffusion nonlinear integer arithmetic prevalent in cryptographic schemes, machine-learning models tend to use limited-precision floating-point arithmetic and low-diffusion linear operations. We show that these operations introduce difficulties in weight recovery, often requiring an unexpectedly large number of traces, even under ideal channel conditions. Second, we observe that, unlike ciphers, which aim to increase the data entropy, machine-learning models aim to reduce it. This reduces data variability as the algorithm progresses, hampering weight recovery in deep layers of the model.

Paper:
title: How To Track Qubits Through Space and Time (Or: Sailing in a Quantum Boat)
summary: While quantum position verification aims to certify a prover's location using quantum information, existing security definitions only guarantee that part of the successful adversarial party is in the claimed location. This leaves open the possibility that a distributed team of adversaries can jointly simulate a prover in a way that defeats the intended meaning of `being at a location' in position-based cryptography. We introduce stronger notions of position verification that we call quantum localization, which requires that there is a specified, unclonable state at the verified spacetime point-and that this state can be found nowhere else. We show that quantum localization leads naturally to a meaningful notion of trajectory verification, in which quantum information is verifiably tracked through space and time. We construct quantum localization and trajectory verification protocols using quantum anchor states, which generalize coset states from unclonable cryptography. The security of our schemes is proven in the classical oracle (i.e. ideal obfuscation) model, which can be heuristically instantiated in the plain model using post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation. We also introduce and instantiate the concept of functionality localization, which guarantees that the adversary has the ability to compute a secret function at the verified spacetime point, and this function cannot be computed anywhere else. This raises the intriguing possibility of localizing computational capabilities in space and time. More broadly, we believe our notions of quantum localization and subsequent feasibility results provide stronger foundations for position-based cryptography. At a conceptual level, our results also explore the tight link between two fundamental notions in physics-location and information-thus serving as a natural foundation for cryptographic capabilities tied to physical spacetime.

Paper:
title: Resetting-based designated information distribution
summary: For a network of $n$ nodes under random gossip dynamics, we show that by introducing the additional resetting mechanism (with rate $β$) to a designated subset of $r$ nodes, the expected sum of all node values is asymptotically equal to $\tfrac{n}{r}$ times the sum of the initial values of the $r$ designated nodes, in the small-$β$ and long-time limit. We also analyze the convergence speed to this asymptotic state and provide an approximate high-probability confidence interval for the expected sum at finite time $t$ and finite $β$. Operationally, we propose a protocol that distributes the initial node values over the designated subset evenly (up to a prescribed precision), by appropriately turning on and off the resetting dynamics. Our work not only offers insights into classical problems such as distributed computing and network control, but also serves as a potential foundation for designing quantum algorithms that prepare desired states in quantum networks using only local operations.

Paper:
title: Brief introduction to post-quantum cryptography in industrial applications
summary: The development of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is directly motivated by the necessity to secure information in the face of the quantum threat. This paper provides an overview of recent developments relevant to PQC adoption across several industrial applications, including IoT, healthcare, civil and infrastructure engineering, and defense. We present a brief, self-contained overview of PQC and its market positioning. We perform implementation experiments on selected quantum-safe methods and quantify several aspects, such as the quantum resources required to break common cryptographic schemes, as well as the performance of the most well-known PQC algorithms. We also discuss the resistance of different PQC classes to quantum attacks and the status of PQC implementations in different programming languages. Finally, we present benchmark results on KEMs and signature algorithms to help select the appropriate algorithm for a specific application based on criteria such as algorithm performance, data lifetime, and level of data sensitivity.

Paper:
title: AutoPYara: Next-Gen YARA Rule Generator for Malware Family Clustering
summary: Millions of malware variants threaten users daily, such that clustering these samples is key for fast incident response. AutoYara is the current state-of-the-art for automatic YARA rule generation, but the task remains challenging on realistic datasets, where intra-family diversity and noisy clustering can degrade rule quality. We present AutoPYara, a solution armored with: (1) precise cluster centroid selection based on similarity hashing, and (2) an improved heuristic for estimating subclusters within a malware family using historical VirusTotal data. We implement AutoPYara as an open-source Python package (pip install autopyara) to support reproducibility and practical use. We show that AutoPYara, (1) increases rule coverage by 14 percentage points; (2) reduces variance by 7.1 percentage points, comparing the average variance AutoPYara exhibits to that of AutoYara; and (3) improves threat-hunting accuracy by 10%. AutoPYara produces robust and effective YARA rules than prior automatic approaches in practical settings.

Paper:
title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
summary: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection.
  To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests.
  We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12386v1

Paper:
title: Detecting Shadow AI: Unsanctioned LLM Agents on Enterprise Endpoints: A Taxonomy, an Open Detector and a Controlled Evaluation
summary: Shadow IT, the use of technology that the IT organisation has not approved, is a long-standing governance problem. We argue that autonomous AI agents can make it grow much faster: agents make building tools nearly free, act with their user's privileges, and leave behind scripts, automations and MCP servers that are themselves unsanctioned. A simple compounding model shows that, under its assumptions, shadow IT grows exponentially once agentic artifacts reproduce faster than the organisation retires them; retiring them starts with detecting them. We then ask whether unsanctioned agents can be detected on Windows endpoints. We propose a taxonomy of nine classes of agents and six layers of endpoint footprint, and argue that rules based only on the structure of processes and connections cannot separate an agent from its behavioural twin, the same program talking to a non-AI service. We present Agent Detector, an open-source Windows detector that anchors behaviour to the identity of the remote service and correlates it with configuration, installation and execution history, using a catalog of 39 tools and 184 LLM endpoint entries; it informs users through a notice they must acknowledge instead of blocking. On a controlled bench of 12 synthetic agents, 3 AI components and 9 benign workloads, repeated 5 times on one workstation, two behavioural rules flagged every behavioural twin, while Agent Detector flagged none and detected every agent in the majority of runs. Its limits are temporal: a connection to a provider behind a shared content-delivery network is attributable only while the DNS cache holds the provider's name, one to five minutes, and an intermittent agent was seen by about one scan in three. A scan costs about 154 ms. The bench is too small to rank detectors; it maps what each kind of evidence can see: unsanctioned agents can be partly detected, and not by behaviour alone.

Paper:
title: Adapting Multi-Stage Distributed Real-Time Systems Design to Vehicular Edge Computing
summary: Vehicular Edge Computing (VEC) aims to support computation-intensive applications in intelligent transportation systems while meeting stringent latency requirements. When processed remotely, applications require access to different resource types in a specific sequence, forming a multi-stage processing pipeline. Paper:
title: An Agile Homomorphic Encryption and ML-KEM Scheme for Privacy-Preserving Health Data Processing
summary: The storage and processing of health data raise serious privacy concerns; therefore, the data must be encrypted. Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) allows computations on encrypted data, which makes it a very promising technology in this context. Paper:
title: Release Sooner, Expose Less: Offloading MoE Dispatch in NCCL-EP under Dual-Batch Overlap
summary: Dual-batch overlap (DBO) hides mixture-of-experts (MoE) communication behind another microbatch's computation, but only after dispatch send releases the GPU. The time dispatch send holds the GPU therefore stays exposed, while network progress after release can be hidden. We evaluate three research configurations built on NCCL-EP that target this exposed communication time: GPI, in which the GPU constructs GPU-Friendly Descriptors (GFDs) and submits them to NIC-accessible memory for transport; GPI-MC, which describes MoE token fan-out in one GFD; and GDAKI Free Flow, which moves send progression to a host thread. On a GB300 NVL72 system, all three approaches reduce dispatch-send time relative to default GDAKI over most operating points in the evaluated parameter sweep. An experiment that inserts a GPU delay between dispatch send and receive shows that offload increases the in-flight interval. Depending on the configuration, 32 to 512 microseconds of computation or other independent work between send and receive hides the deferred progress, leaving less exposed time than default GDAKI. In disaggregated vLLM serving with DBO, these approaches lower median TPOT by 15-25% relative to NCCL-EP default GDAKI and by 16-42% relative to DeepEP v1.

Paper:
title: An Explicit Below Half Threshold Bound for the Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir's Secret Sharing Scheme
summary: As a fundamental cryptographic primitive, secret sharing distributes a secret among multiple parties and allows certain authorized parties to recover the secret while preventing unauthorized parties from knowing the secret. However, local leakage from each party member allows an adversary to learn partial information from each share, which is not guaranteed by traditional security. In this paper, we study bounds on the reconstruction threshold of Shamir's secret sharing scheme over prime fields against arbitrary 1-bit local leakage. We show that, for all sufficiently large $n$ and every prime $p>n$, the $(n,t)$-Shamir's scheme is $\exp(-Ω(n))$-resilient whenever $t/n\geq 0.489$, for any choice of distinct nonzero evaluation points. Our proof refines the dual-code list recovery analysis and combines complementary Fourier estimates according to the support sizes and biases of the leakage functions, yielding an improved explicit reconstruction threshold bound.

Paper:
title: Mitigating SM-Level Load Imbalance in 3D Gaussian Splatting on GPUs
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables photorealistic, real-time rendering on commodity GPUs and is increasingly adopted in generative world models and autonomous driving simulators. However, existing optimizations rely on algorithmic changes that often require retraining, or on specialized accelerators that lack flexibility across evolving 3DGS variants. In this paper, we identify a fundamental inefficiency in GPU-based 3DGS rendering: severe SM-level load imbalance caused by uneven workloads across screen tiles. This imbalance creates a long execution tail, leaving most SMs idle while a few process computationally intensive tiles, particularly in large-scale urban scenes. To address this, we present a software-defined GPU scheduling approach that mitigates the execution tail. Our approach uses a persistent kernel to schedule heavy tiles first and selectively chunks outlier tiles across multiple CTAs. A lightweight per-frame policy determines when and how much to chunk using tile statistics already available in the rendering pipeline. Our approach requires neither retraining nor specialized hardware and can be applied orthogonally to existing optimizations across diverse 3DGS variants. Averaged per scene, it accelerates alpha blending by up to 2.93x on a large-scale urban scene, and by up to 5.6x on its most imbalanced frames, while retaining the original alpha blending formulation.

Paper:
title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
summary: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. Paper:
title: RecoGEM: A Serving System for Production-Scale Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) is moving industrial recommender systems (RecSys) from scoring candidate items to autoregressively generating item identifiers. This shift promises higher recommendation quality, but makes serving substantially harder: each request executes a short sequence of dependent decoding steps that explore a large item space and select promising candidates on the latency-critical path. GR not only creates structural mismatches with conventional RecSys pipelines, but also challenges the architectural and optimization assumptions of LLM serving stacks, making direct adoption of existing systems difficult. We present RecoGEM, our production GR serving system. RecoGEM uses a runtime--engine decoupling architecture to move GR-specific serving responsibilities, such as candidate-state transitions and live artifact updates, to a dedicated runtime. Its execution engine exploits GR's short token sequences, large candidate populations, and predictable step shapes to optimize self-attention, candidate selection, and execution planning. RecoGEM has been deployed for over nine months across our production lines, serving applications with hundreds of millions of users and supporting more than ten GR model families. On our OneModel production workloads, RecoGEM reaches over 1,000 QPS per serving instance with P99 latency below 35 ms and a 2.88$\times$ throughput improvement over representative baselines.

Paper:
title: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agentic AI frameworks connect language models to external tool providers, but it carries attacker-controlled content (tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data) into model context without validation. Prior benchmarks measure model compliance with poisoned instructions without confirming real execution. We present the first cross-framework measurement of MCP tool poisoning with real tool execution. A 25-class root-cause taxonomy unifies prior classifications, and the open-source tool mcpvenom drives a 9,720-cell susceptibility matrix across 12 frameworks, 18 models, and 45 attack scenarios, with a dual oracle that confirms exfiltration via canary HTTP receipt. The overall attack success rate is 22.9% (2,113 vulnerable cells). Of these, 64.9% dispatch an attacker tool call, 23.0% contact the attacker endpoint, and 12.1% verifiably exfiltrate a secret. Resistance is model-level: nine core frameworks cluster within 23 to 26% (chi-squared = 3.30, p = 0.91), and no framework implements intentional defense. Incidental framework properties mitigate in specific cases, and a regex description scanner rejects 20 of 45 scenarios at a 7.2% false-positive rate, so metadata scanning alone is a partial control. Model ASR ranges from 0.4% to 49.7%. Claude Opus 4.8 is vulnerable in 8 of 530 cells while issuing 223 explicit refusals. A code-level audit finds no intentional defense across twelve frameworks, and all five coordinated disclosures across four vendors were rejected.

Paper:
title: Public, Identifiable, and Effectively Immutable: Ethical Lessons from Research on arXiv
summary: Ethical decision-making is central to safe cybersecurity research. Recent studies, one of which is our own, analyzing the source files of arXiv papers bring this challenge to light - arXiv publicly distributes the source files, to the surprise of many authors. Unique aspects reveal ethical challenges and dilemmas that extend beyond established ethical frameworks, institutional processes, and community best practices. In this work, we examine this case and provide insights for similar research on other public live resources, such as Zenodo or the Wayback Machine. title: Lessons Not Learned: Why Cross-Chain Bridges Keep Losing Billions the Same Way
summary: Bridge hacks have cost billions, often without exploiting a code bug. title: SNAPRAG: Cost-Efficient Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems via Adversarial Perturbations
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve Large Language Model (LLM) responses by incorporating information from external knowledge bases. However, recent studies have shown that attackers can extract substantial portions of private knowledge bases from RAG systems through repeated querying. title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
summary: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by output-length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while reducing fluctuations in the supply of generated samples to the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Within our asynchronous architecture, ASP's scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. The complete system improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. It also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.

Paper:
title: Optimal Proximity Black Hole Search with Programmable Matter
summary: The concept of programmable matter (PM) envisions objects composed of tiny, mobile particles capable of self-arrangement, which allows them to change shape, color, and move.
  We initiate the study of the Black Hole Search problem within the context of PM. The problem involves a dangerous and unnoticeable location, the black hole, that, without a trace, destroys any particle visiting it. In our setting, particles move inside a convex area embedded in a triangular grid, where one vertex is a black hole. The objective is for the particles to identify a restricted set of vertices containing the black hole while ensuring that at least one particle survives.
  We present an algorithm utilizing three particles capable of assuming just two colors to identify the dangerous region where the black hole resides. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this algorithm is Pareto optimal in terms of number of particles and number of colors required, and asymptotically optimal in terms of number of epochs, where an epoch refers to the minimal time window within which each particle completed an activation cycle at least once.

Paper:
title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
summary: Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.

Paper:
title: GPU-Accelerated Non-Interactive Encrypted Neural Network Training with Batched Diagonal Packing
summary: Training a neural network under homomorphic encryption requires transposes, batch reductions, optimizer updates, and repeated refreshes in addition to forward matrix products. We combine rectangular diagonal packing, feature-major SIMD mini-batch lanes, baby-step giant-step evaluation, and compact optimizer state in an MIT-licensed Rust CKKS implementation. Its CUDA path keeps training and bootstrap ciphertext arithmetic on the GPU, while retaining host key generation and client operations. In a matched 100-update experiment on the main non-interactive MNIST model, device-resident bootstrapping reduces training time from 14,268.295 to 293.075 seconds, a $48.68\times$ ratio against our CPU implementation, with exactly equal decoded parameters and predictions. Including setup and final evaluation gives a $40.67\times$ ratio. A separate GPU run completes ten passes over 4,800 images in 2,967.095 seconds and achieves 90.35% test accuracy versus 90.41% for its plaintext twin. These are single-initialization results; exact CPU/GPU parameter agreement is verified at 100 updates, not for the full 1,000-update run. Earlier completed CPU runs support a larger-batch key-switch advantage and baseline-batch accuracy within the registered tolerance, but the baseline-batch normalized key-switch target is missed. The released ReBoot baseline does not meet the common security-estimator threshold, and its full-setting CPU time is unmeasured. We therefore distinguish measured acceleration of our implementation from conditional layout comparisons and do not claim unconditional superiority over ReBoot.

Paper:
title: StealthyPoison: Manipulating LLM Agent Behavior through Procedural Poisoning of Third-Party Skills
summary: LLM agents increasingly retrieve third-party skills from public registries and follow their procedures to complete user tasks. This reliance allows attackers to manipulate agent behavior by poisoning the skills. However, overtly malicious instructions can provide explicit signals for detection. We present StealthyPoison, a stealthy procedural poisoning attack that corrupts a skill's decision-critical rules to induce incorrect task outcomes while preserving its advertised functionality and normal execution. Unlike prior knowledge corruption attacks that craft poisoned content for known target question-answer pairs, StealthyPoison constructs reusable poisoned procedures from a publicly available third-party skill, without access to actual user requests or their ground-truth answers. To make the poisoned procedure generalize to unseen requests, it first synthesizes requests from the target skill and executes its clean version using a surrogate agent to obtain pseudo-references. These references and surrogate execution feedback guide the iterative refinement of payloads that alter decision-critical rules. To increase the likelihood that the poisoned skill is retrieved and selected over benign alternatives, the attack augments the poisoned skill's retrieval metadata with independently generated request descriptions. We evaluate StealthyPoison on 566 eligible target skills and 5,244 requests against more than 26,000 registry entries. It improves top-1 poisoned-skill placement by 13.6% relative to both HotFlip and GCG. Constructed using feedback from a single surrogate model, the procedural poisoning payloads transfer effectively and without modification to three held-out victim models and achieve end-to-end attack success in a Claude Code workflow powered by Opus 4.8. The defense evaluation further shows that most of these payloads evade detection by both SkillSpector and GPT-5.4-mini.

Paper:
title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
summary: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as BF16 and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52x and 1.48x over the fastest baseline on an RTX 4060 Ti and an RTX 5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.

Paper:
title: Honeyval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for LLM-powered HTTP Honeypots
summary: Honeypots are decoy systems mimicking real system components designed to defend against cyber attacks. Recently, LLMs increasingly serve as simulation backbones for honeypots. They enable defenders to construct high-interaction honeypots with low system security risks. However, LLM-powered honeypot development lacks a unified evaluation framework. Most evaluations consist of measuring response similarity on fixed commands, manual testing, or real-world deployment. These methods are often not scalable for development, reproducible across evaluations, representative of practical attacks, or adaptable to various attacker and honeypot configurations. In this work, we bridge this gap and propose Honeyval, a comprehensive evaluation framework for LLM-powered HTTP honeypots. We address the limitations of prior evaluations by grounding the honeypots in 16 backend applications, using AI hacking agents as attackers, employing two control tasks to monitor agent and honeypot capabilities across customizations, and defining clear and verifiable exploit goals for the attacker. Using Honeyval, we conduct an extensive evaluation of recent cost-efficient LLMs as HTTP honeypots. Our experiments highlight the promise of LLM-powered honeypots; they lead to substantially longer interactions with the attacker than rule-based baseline honeypots and are far less frequently detected even by frontier models, all while, on average, preserving a running cost advantage against agentic attackers. Further, we experiment with various honeypot extensions and counter-offensive configurations, observing unique trade-offs, e.g., lower latency at the price of increased detection.

title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics
summary: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. Paper:
title: Accelerating AIGC Services with Latent Action Diffusion Scheduling in Edge Networks
summary: Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC) has gained significant popularity for creating diverse content. However, current AIGC models primarily focus on content quality within a centralized framework, resulting in a high service delay and negative user experiences. The workload of an AIGC task is determined by model complexity and multi-layered encoder architectures, posing significant challenges for its modeling, deployment, and scheduling within resource-constrained edge networks. We model an offloading problem among edges for providing real AIGC services and propose \textbf{LAD-TS}, a novel Latent Action Diffusion-based Task Scheduling method that orchestrates multiple edge servers for expedited AIGC services by leveraging the diffusion model's conditional guidance capability and the reinforcement learning's environment interaction ability. We first design an innovative Latent Action Diffusion Network (LADN) model based on traditional diffusion models. We then incorporate the LADN model into deep reinforcement learning, forming an effective LAD-TS method for task scheduling in distributed edge networks. Meanwhile, we design a latent action diffusion strategy to achieve near-optimal decisions quickly by utilizing historical action probabilities instead of Gaussian noise. Furthermore, we implement a refined AIGC model and develop \textbf{DEdgeAI}, a prototype edge system with the refined AIGC model deployment to evaluate our LAD-TS method. DEdgeAI provides a real AIGC service for users, demonstrating up to $7.36\%-18.11\%$ and $34.07\%-94.96\%$ shorter service delays than the state-of-the-art methods and representative commercial platforms, respectively. We release our open-source code at https://github.com/ChangfuXu/DEdgeAI/

title: A Privacy-Preserving UAV-Assisted Secure Wireless Communication and Computing System Based on Fully Homomorphic Encryption
summary: With the advancement of beyond-5G networks, privacy-preserving communication and secure computation face critical challenges due to the openness of wireless channels. Existing security mechanisms protect data transmission but fail to secure the computation process itself. In this paper, we propose a UAV-assisted secure computing framework that integrates Cheon Kim Kim Song (CKKS) fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) with multi-party secure computation (MPC). Paper:
title: ShiftCache: Fast and Exact Indel Effect Prediction by Reusing Shifted Reference Encodings
summary: Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi read up to a megabase of DNA and score a genetic variant by comparing their predictions for the reference and alternate sequences. Insertions and deletions (indels) are costly to score, because an indel usually shifts the unchanged DNA after it onto a different pooling grid, which prevents direct reuse of the reference's encoder activations. The AlphaGenome Atlas scored more than 100 million indels with three full model passes each, although the DNA after an indel matches the reference shifted by the indel's length. We present ShiftCache, an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference once and shares it among all variants scored in the same window with the same shift. ShiftCache copies every encoder output a variant can reuse and recomputes the rest in batched tiles. On held-out AlphaGenome windows shared by many indels, in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7$\times$ faster than our adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse to indels. It is 3.5 to 4.1$\times$ faster than dense reimplementations of two published analyses with Borzoi and AlphaGenome, and 2.6$\times$ faster than dense execution with Enformer. Scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window makes ShiftCache only 1.36$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution, and highly diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits can make it slower than layer-by-layer reuse or dense execution. For encoders that meet our conditions, ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic. On an A6000, every checked output of the default AlphaGenome and Borzoi runs matches dense execution within an absolute and relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$. With larger tile batches, with Enformer or on an H100, a small fraction of values exceeds this tolerance.

Paper:
title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
summary: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured.
  To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations.
  Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

Paper:
title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.

Paper:
title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
summary: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.

Paper:
title: Improved Scaling for Fast Mode of Ozaki Scheme II
summary: Ozaki scheme II emulates high-precision matrix multiplication using low-precision integer matrix operations based on the Chinese remainder theorem (CRT). It first scales the high-precision matrices to convert them into integer matrices. For this scaling step, Ozaki scheme II provides two modes: accurate mode, which uses INT8 matrix multiplication to estimate scaling factors, and fast mode, which applies the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality at lower computational cost. We show that the existing formula lacks scale invariance; multiplying the input matrices by a constant changes the effective bit width of the integer matrices in the scaling step, causing accuracy degradation or CRT recovery failure. To address this, we propose a revised scaling formula derived from the CRT uniqueness condition via the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. The proposed formula is scale-invariant by construction, guarantees that the CRT uniqueness condition is always satisfied, and introduces no additional overhead over the original fast mode. Experiments on an NVIDIA GH200 GPU show that the proposed method achieves accuracy comparable to that of accurate mode while maintaining throughput comparable to that of fast mode. In the accuracy--throughput trade-off, the proposed method overcomes the accuracy limitation of fast mode and the throughput constraint of accurate mode, offering a superior accuracy and performance.

Paper:
title: Accelerating Direct Sparse Solvers with Graph Computing Accelerators
summary: Solving large sparse linear systems by Gaussian elimination is a challenging computational task due to the introduction of non-zero elements, or fill-in. Practitioners use heuristics such as the nested dissection reordering algorithm to try to reduce fill-in. Paper:
title: DeFSM: Robust and Efficient Decentralization of Federated Submodular Maximization
summary: Submodular maximization seeks a small subset best representing a large dataset. In its federated setting, the server is a single point of failure and some clients may be Byzantine. Removing the server raises a trilemma of decentraliza- tion, efficiency, and security. We propose DeFSM, a Byzantine-robust and communication-efficient architecture that replaces the server with a lightweight smart contract and a pool of independent, consensus-free agents. Its aggregation rule, SafeGM, builds on two notions from combinatorial geometry: Tukey depth and safe points (the points lying in the convex hull of the good points wherever the bad points are). SafeGM makes the robust decision on 2D Gaussian random projections, which the contract can compute efficiently, and lifts it back as a convex combination of actual updates. Since lifting loses information, it uses the projected geometric median only when its depth certifies it, and otherwise a Tukey median. The share of bad updates is then bounded only by a count: how many there are, not what they contain. We prove, and confirm empirically, that this bound controls the solution quality. On CIFAR10 and PathMNIST, with up to 30% Byzantine clients and agents, DeFSM never collapses and retains on average about 91% of the quality of the ideal reference, the geometric median at a trusted central server. The geometric median decentralized in its best setting would retain about 96%, but the contract cannot compute it, and so each agent would have to download six times more data, or each client twice as much.
