Paper:
title: Expanding Codes with Polynomial Stretch
summary: We give a polynomial-stretch, constant-arity counterpart to the expanding-code construction of Blasiok, Lou, Rosen, and Sudan (FOCS 2026). For every constant $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, we construct binary matrices with $n$ columns and polynomially many rows, each of weight $k=O(\varepsilon^{-6})$, such that the union of the supports of any set of at most $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ rows has size at least $(1-\varepsilon)k$ times the number of rows. Nevertheless, a polynomial-time test accepts every codeword (generated by the columns of this matrix) corrupted in at most a $1/2-\varepsilon$ fraction of its coordinates, while rejecting a uniformly random vector with high probability.
  We give two applications. First, we obtain a family of (nearly lossless) constant locality expanders on which Goldreich's pseudorandom generator with the XOR-MAJ predicate can be distinguished from uniform in polynomial time, well within the small-bias parameter regime and the hard regime for known algebraic-immunity/annihilator attacks and algebraic-degree linearization attacks described by Applebaum and Lovett (STOC 2016, SICOMP 2018).
  Second, we obtain public key encryption from either the constant-noise $k$XOR conjecture over random graphs or the Goldreich conjecture with XOR-MAJ over random graphs, together with a new planted-hypergraph conjecture. We prove low-degree lower bounds for the planting conjecture, providing evidence for subexponential hardness, and give lower bounds against dimension tests based on coordinatewise products (Schur products) of public-code vectors.

Paper:
title: Embedded Blockchain Infrastructure Management (eBIM): A RISC-V-Empowered Hardware--Software Co-Design Framework Towards Trustworthy Blockchain
summary: Blockchain systems are shifting from decentralized ledgers for digital assets to general-purpose trust infrastructures for verifiable computation, decentralized physical resources, and automated infrastructure management. However, deploying these systems through third-party Blockchain-as-a-Service (BaaS) offerings may introduce dependencies involving operational control, confidentiality, and infrastructure governance. Meanwhile, blockchain execution and verification impose demanding requirements on cryptographic processing, isolation, and reproducibility. RISC-V offers an open, extensible instruction set architecture that enables co-design of software execution environments and domain-specific security hardware. Inspired by the embedded identity and provisioning model of an embedded subscriber identity module (eSIM), this survey proposes embedded Blockchain infrastructure management (eBIM) as a conceptual hardware-software co-design framework that organizes existing RISC-V-enabled technologies into a hardware-anchored blockchain infrastructure stack. We systematically review RISC-V-based smart-contract execution, trusted execution environments, zero-knowledge virtual machines, and cryptographic acceleration, and analyze their relationship to blockchain requirements, including deterministic execution, verifiability, extensibility, and secure key management. Based on this evidence, we distinguish currently demonstrated capabilities from the proposed eBIM integration vision and identify major open challenges, including system-level benchmarking, blockchain-oriented cryptographic extensions, TEE security, post-quantum migration, and deployable hardware-software co-design. The survey provides an architectural reference for researchers and designers investigating open and verifiable blockchain infrastructure.

Paper:
title: Track or Follow? A Jev-Compatible Multi-Agent Trading System When Web News Lags the Market
summary: LLM agents increasingly trade on the Web news they read, yet much Web news about listed firms is published after, and about, the price move it reports, so a reader can agree with the market by following it instead of reading the event. We ask whether LLM judgments of Web news track the market's reaction to the reported event or follow it. To answer, we built a multi-agent trading system whose agents share only point-in-time stores and answer typed questions through the interface of Jev, a hosted typed decision model; code sets every position under a proved bound on how far text can move it. In a hash-committed test of a Jev-compatible reader built from a pinned LLM's option probabilities, item judgments track announcement-window abnormal returns (weekly Spearman 0.119), also after the LLM's release, and event types agree with the issuers' 8-K filings (AUC 0.833); Jev's judgments of news published after its own release track the reaction as well (descriptive). Exploratory analyses show where the association comes from: 72% of earnings news items appear after the issuer's filing, contributor-written items often report the price move, and from the first trade after publication the association falls to 0.023. At a weekly horizon, the confirmatory test detects no rank information over code-only features. Under attack, decision cards traced 88% of successful attacks to the planted item. We propose that market-graded tests of Web-text readers report the criterion from publication, not only from the event.

summary: For every constant $c > 0$, we unconditionally construct witness encryption for NP in the classical generic cyclic group model with the following properties. Paper:
title: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
summary: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. Designed for quorum-based systems, QUASI enables parties to attest to external entities that the statement is valid. Surprisingly, each party need not sign the entire statement: authenticating only a small subset of symbols suffices for the quorum to attest to the whole. A simple deterministic construction illustrates this possibility. Built purely from hashing and error correction, QUASI achieves small per-party contributions and low attestation generation and verification costs, without relying on SNARKs for aggregation.
  Our main contribution is a randomized construction achieving reductions of more than $10\times$ in per-party contribution size and hash computations for generation and verification, compared with full hash-based signatures.
  QUASI is a generic primitive supporting diverse applications. Two principal use cases are external attestation for signature-free consensus, enabling clients to verify statements about committed state; and preprocessing for SNARK-based aggregation, compounding QUASI's savings with succinct-proof compression.

Paper:
title: Language-Based Agent Control
summary: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control. In conventional programming, combinations of static typing and runtime enforcement have long been used to guarantee that well-typed programs satisfy user-specified policies, including policies for access control, information flow, data provenance, and more. The key idea behind LBAC is to extend these guarantees to agentic applications by requiring agents to generate programs that are themselves well-typed in the context of the surrounding scaffolding code. Unsafe programs are rejected by the typechecker before execution, allowing policies to apply uniformly across the entire application, including both agent-generated behavior and developer-written scaffolding. Paper:
title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation
summary: LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.

Paper:
title: The Limits of Information-Flow Control Enforcement for Agentic Systems
summary: Information-flow control (IFC) is a promising approach to enforce policy in agentic AI systems. However, IFC suffers from label creep, a phenomenon where monotonically increasing security labels propagate through a system and progressively limit its utility. Label creep in agentic AI systems can be mitigated using two major strategies: (1) improved system design and (2) label declassification. In this paper, we characterize how far system design alone can mitigate label creep in agentic systems. Specifically, we measure how system topology, scale, and agent composition affect utility loss and security enforcement cost proxies for conservative IFC enforcement in a stateful agentic system simulator. We develop a pipeline to systematically vary these features and measure their impacts on label propagation. Our results demonstrate strong associations between structural graph features and our IFC utility loss metric (up to a Spearman correlation $|ρ|$ of $0.96$) and show that system size and tool allocation substantially affect how labels propagate. These findings identify design choices to reduce IFC utility loss, but they also demonstrate that system design alone cannot fully prevent utility loss due to monotonic label propagation. This motivates the development of label declassification mechanisms that aid these design choices and diminish IFC utility cost.

Paper:
title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
summary: Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand.
  We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings.
  On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.

title: CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data
summary: There is growing awareness that the analysis of personal data, such as individuals' mobility, financial, and health data, can provide significant benefits to society. Paper:
title: When Fancy Eviction Fails: Rethinking Cache Replacement For LLM Prefix Reuse
summary: Long-running LLM applications and autonomous agents repeatedly send growing context, making prefix caching critical for reducing prefill cost. This raises a fundamental question: do decades of traditional cache-management techniques transfer directly to agentic and conversational LLM serving? We analyze production traces comprising over 20 billion processed tokens and evaluate 14 eviction algorithms across capacity-constrained HBM and large memory-pool settings. We find that simple Least Recently Used (LRU) is surprisingly robust, offering competitive performance against sophisticated traditional policies, though substantial headroom to Belady's optimum remains. The reason is structural: prefix reuse is dominated by the steady pacing of active sessions, making recency an unusually strong predictor for eviction. Nevertheless, prefix caching diverges from traditional workloads in ways that recency ignores, notably the prevalence of single-turn requests, extreme session footprint skew, and highly non-uniform miss costs because attention computation scales with token depth. To close the gap to optimality, we establish several design principles for prefix-cache management: keeping recency as the baseline while incorporating quick demotion to filter one-hit prompts, compute-aware eviction to prioritize expensive misses, and capacity-adaptive eviction granularity. Our traces and simulator are publicly available.

title: Claudini: Autoresearch Discovers State-of-the-Art Adversarial Attack Algorithms for LLMs
summary: We show that AI agents are capable of discovering novel algorithms for adversarial attacks against LLMs, advancing the state of the art on white-box jailbreaking and prompt injection evaluations. We deploy frontier agents, such as Claude Code and Codex, in an autoresearch loop with access to a library of 30+ prior methods and an evaluation script with a fixed compute budget. For SecAlign, it achieves 100\% ASR, while the best prior automated methods only achieve 82\%. Notably, in our setting, attack methods are developed on unrelated surrogate models for a pure random-target token-forcing task, yet generalize directly to prompt injection on the adversarially trained model. Finally, we trace the lineage of methods developed during autoresearch, characterizing the agents' strategies and failure modes. Adversarial ML has long held that defenses must be evaluated against attacks tailored to them; autoresearch automates this principle, and we argue it should be the minimum bar for defense evaluation going forward.

title: Reproducible LoRA Inference Through Deterministic Split-K Reduction
summary: Reproducibility is important for LoRA-adapted language models used in repeated evaluation, auditing, and decision-making. Paper:
title: Inquisitive Team Semantics of LTL
summary: In recent years, hyperproperties (i.e., properties of sets of traces) have been identified as a crucial concept for capturing information-flow security policies and knowledge of agents in distributed systems. In the synchronous linear-time setting, a well-known approach for the specification of hyperproperties is based on the set semantics of standard LTL. The resulting logic (TeamLTL) inherits the powerful split interpretation of disjunction from dependence logic. In this paper, we introduce a novel team semantics of LTL inspired by inquisitive logic, whose main features are the intuitionistic interpretation of implication and the inquisitive semantics of disjunction. We investigate expressiveness, decidability, and complexity issues of the novel logic that we call InqLTL and its extension with strong negation. We show that InqLTL with strong negation is highly undecidable and strictly less expressive than TeamLTL with strong negation. On the positive side, we identify a meaningful fragment of InqLTL with a decidable model-checking problem that can express relevant classes of hyperproperties. To the best of our knowledge, this fragment represents the first hyper logic with a decidable model-checking problem that allows unrestricted use of temporal modalities and conditional second-order universal quantification over system refinements via intuitionistic implication.

Paper:
title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-ased Management of Continuum Resources
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. Paper:
title: Testing CCZ-equivalence to permutations via projections of Walsh zero spaces, with applications to APN functions
summary: Whether almost perfect nonlinear (APN) permutations exist in even dimension $n\ge 8$ is a long-standing open question, the big APN problem. The only example known in even dimension, on six bits, was found from a quadratic APN function that is not itself a permutation, by Carlet--Charpin--Zinoviev (CCZ) equivalence. It is therefore natural to test APN functions for CCZ-equivalence to a permutation. This amounts to finding two complementary $n$-dimensional subspaces among the zeros of the Walsh transform, which lie in $\mathbb{F}_2^{2n}$. A known necessary condition only uses their projections to $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and cannot decide every case. We give an exact test for functions whose Walsh supports are affine, including all quadratic functions. It reconstructs the subspaces from their projections, through searches for subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and for constrained bilinear maps. On the benchmarked functions in dimension twelve, it lists them $39$ to $55$ times faster than the generic search of the commonly used sboxU library. We then study the functions $x^3+a^{-1}\mathrm{Tr}(a^3x^9)$, which Göloğlu and Pavlů proved not to be CCZ-equivalent to permutations when $4$ divides $n$. With their result, our computations show that this holds for every even $n\le 24$. In dimension $18$ the necessary condition is satisfied, and the new test decides the case. We conjecture this for every even dimension. We also compile $25$ classes of quadratic APN functions in dimension ten from published instances, with equivalence certificates. No function in these classes or in their switching closure is CCZ-equivalent to a permutation. All code and data are public.

Paper:
title: MUSE: Multi-Tenant Model Serving With Seamless Model Updates
summary: In binary classification systems, decision thresholds translate model scores into actions. Choosing suitable thresholds relies on the specific distribution of the underlying model scores but also on the specific business decisions of each client using that model. However, retraining models inevitably shifts score distributions, invalidating existing thresholds. In multi-tenant Score-as-a-Service environments, where decision boundaries reside in client-managed infrastructure, this creates a severe bottleneck: recalibration requires coordinating threshold updates across hundreds of clients, consuming excessive human hours and leading to model stagnation. We introduce MUSE, a model serving framework that enables seamless model updates by decoupling model scores from client decision boundaries. Designed for multi-tenancy, MUSE optimizes infrastructure re-use by sharing models via dynamic intent-based routing, combined with a two-level score transformation that maps model outputs to a stable, reference distribution. Deployed at scale by Feedzai, MUSE processes over a thousand events per second, and over 55 billion events in the last 12 months, across several dozens of tenants, while maintaining high-availability and low-latency guarantees. By reducing model lead time from weeks to minutes, MUSE promotes model resilience against shifting attacks, saving millions of dollars in fraud losses and operational costs.

Paper:
title: FirstSwap: Pre-Consensus Trade Approvals for Decentralized Market Design
summary: Decentralized exchanges typically give traders no execution guarantee until a block is finalized. In the meantime, external prices move, traders strategically delay submission, and block producers can influence inclusion and ordering. We introduce FirstSwap, a DEX built on a constant-function market maker pricing curve that gives traders an early pre-approval before consensus, guaranteeing inclusion and execution within their submitted price limit, with final ordering determined by limit prices rather than by a block producer.
  We demonstrate the benefits of trade pre-approvals in an economic model combining auction theory with CEX-DEX arbitrage. When the CEX price changes gradually, FirstSwap rewards earlier traders with better prices, discouraging strategic delay and yielding higher social welfare and gains to AMM liquidity providers than a batch auction. When the CEX price jumps abruptly, FirstSwap yields higher welfare and smaller AMM losses than fair ordering.
  The central challenge is delivering fast trade pre-approvals without consensus. We introduce a decentralized, scaled admissibility protocol under which each validator reserves only a fraction of the available liquidity at every price. A trader obtains approval in a single round of messages with a quorum of validators. Somewhat surprisingly, despite Byzantine validators who may approve trades arbitrarily, we show that all quorum-certified trades are jointly admissible and execute within their limits. Our protocol extends naturally to a setting where buy and sell orders can be pre-approved against each other before a block is finalized.

Paper:
title: PACE: Keeping the Right Tokens in the KV Cache Is Not Enough for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.

Paper:
title: Vectorized Dynamic Histograms for Sparse Oblique Forests
summary: Sparse oblique (SPO), part of the top-ranked configuration of Google's Yggdrasil Decision Forests (YDF), improve the accuracy while maintaining interpretability of Random Forests (RF) and Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT) by scanning a sparse linear combination of features instead of a single feature. Our optimizations bring SPO-RF training time on par with YDF's axis-aligned RF. We extensively evaluate on 8 natural and 11 synthetic datasets of up to 10.5 million rows and 1.6 million features, from depth 6 to purity, and open-source the implementation.

Paper:
title: Sampling-Free Privacy Accounting for Matrix Mechanisms under Random Allocation
summary: We study privacy amplification for differentially private model training with matrix factorization under random allocation (also known as the balls-in-bins model). Recent work by Choquette-Choo et al. (2025) proposes a sampling-based Monte Carlo approach to compute amplification parameters in this setting. However, their guarantees either only hold with some high probability or require random abstention by the mechanism. Furthermore, the required number of samples for ensuring $(ε,δ)$-DP is inversely proportional to $δ$. In contrast, we develop sampling-free bounds based on Rényi divergence and conditional composition. The former is facilitated by a dynamic programming formulation to efficiently compute the bounds. The latter complements it by offering stronger privacy guarantees for small $ε$, where Rényi divergence bounds inherently lead to an over-approximation. Our framework applies to arbitrary banded and non-banded matrices. Through numerical comparisons, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach across a broad range of matrix mechanisms used in research and practice.

Paper:
title: GSynPEF: A Privacy Evaluation Framework for Synthetic Graphs
summary: It is often desirable to generate and release synthetic graphs, which resemble real-world data, in a privacy-preserving way. While substantial progress has been made in designing private graph synthesizers (PGS), opportunities remain for more explicit connections between synthesizer models and privacy evaluation, and better accounting for output variation. This paper proposes GSynPEF, a practical framework for empirical evaluation of privacy and utility in settings for which a real-world graph is given as input and output synthetic graph(s) are observed. Our framework links a broad class of graph synthesizers (both statistical and deep-learning based) with privacy metrics, expanding evaluation dimensions to practical utility and risk, through empirical analysis of multiple actual outputs. The framework accommodates both an Exact Solution scenario, where synthesizer behavior is directly observable, and a Monte Carlo Approximation scenario where only synthetic outputs from a black box synthesizer are available. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets and seven widely used graph synthesizers demonstrate framework's versatility, enabling privacy evaluation for different attack goals (e.g., to infer an edge or node) and capabilities (e.g., observing one or multiple synthetic graphs). We analyze evaluation results by examining the relationship between graph statistics and synthesizer design choices, providing insights for data curators in PGS selection and researchers for improved PGS design.

Paper:
title: BACGUARD: Fact-Grounded Runtime Mitigation of Broken Access Control
summary: Broken Access Control (BAC) has been the foremost category in the OWASP Top Ten since 2021, primarily due to the challenges in enforcing authorization at the application layer. Traditional mechanisms depend on logic embedded in the application, referencing relational database information such as permissions, roles, or ownership. However, missing or incorrect checks can go undetected by external systems, leaving applications vulnerable. This paper presents BACGUARD, a reverse proxy designed to enforce authorization for unmodified applications. BACGUARD reconstructs authorization relations by leveraging authenticated user data from session stores and object ownership from relational schemas. It evaluates whether users are permitted to access resources and blocks unauthorized requests in real time. Unlike existing approaches, BACGUARD bases its authorization on database joins, making the system resilient to forgery. For most requests, decisions are made deterministically. In cases where access control violations are only apparent in response data, such as cross-user data leakage, a language model is used as a fallback. Evaluations on six applications, including those with known vulnerabilities, demonstrate that BACGUARD's hybrid deterministic and language model-based approach blocks all tested attacks with a false-positive rate below 0.7%. Competing solutions like Web Application Firewalls are less effective and more disruptive. The results highlight BACGUARD's primary contribution: the external reconstruction of authorization facts, enabling robust enforcement even when the application itself is flawed.

Paper:
title: Cryptanalysis of operad-based cryptography
summary: Commutative operads have been proposed as a platform for public-key cryptography, with protocols for key agreement, key exchange, encryption and authentication, together with a masking technique and families of algebras with secret parameters intended to strengthen them. We show that breaking key agreement, key exchange and encryption reduces to two problems over the centralizer of the public operations: an interpolation problem for key agreement and a division problem for the other two. Neither problem requires recovering a secret, and the set from which secrets are drawn plays no role in these attacks. For the operad platforms in the two original papers (fields, the integers, residue rings, the tropical semiring with finite entries, convexors and the masked tropical algebras), the relevant problems can be solved in polynomial time in the input models specified here, and masking does not affect these attacks. The authentication protocol fails for a more elementary reason: as originally stated it does not bind the prover to any public key, and even with a registered public key the response expected by the verifier can be computed from public data. In the masked variant, verification requires the secret mask; on the concrete string platforms, one observed session with an invertible challenge entry suffices for forgery. We also observe that one of the auxiliary constructions satisfies the algebra axioms only in a degenerate case, although the corresponding protocol remains correct. The attacks are implemented and verified on random instances of representative platforms.

title: Cooperate to Compete: Strategic Data Generation and Incentivization Framework for Coopetitive Cross-Silo Federated Learning
summary: In data-sensitive domains such as finance, cross-silo federated learning (CFL) allows organizations to collaboratively train AI models without sharing raw data. However, many practical CFL deployments are coopetitive, where organizations cooperate during model training while competing in downstream markets. In such settings, training contributions can improve the global model yet inadvertently strengthen rivals, eroding one's competitive advantage. This dilemma is amplified by non-IID data, which leads to asymmetric learning gains and undermines sustained participation. While existing work reward organizations based on marginal training contributions, they fail to account for the implicit costs of strengthening competitors. In this paper, we introduce CoCoGen+, a coopetition-compatible data generation and incentivization framework that jointly models data heterogeneity and inter-organizational competition while endogenizing GenAI-based synthetic data generation as a strategic decision. Specifically, CoCoGen+ formulates each training round as a weighted potential game, where organizations strategically decide how much data to generate by balancing learning gains against computational costs and utility losses caused by competition. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the continuous Nash equilibrium under the adopted model and develop a provably convergent scalar bisection algorithm. We further analyze how bilateral payoff redistribution modifies residual competition and data-generation incentives, and empirically evaluate the social welfare and individual utilities of the resulting allocations. Experiments on FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 validate the feasibility of CoCoGen+. The results show how heterogeneity, competition intensity, and incentives shape organizational strategies and social welfare, while CoCoGen+ achieves higher social welfare than competition-aware baselines.
